# The Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

There's a mug in my kitchen that's been half-full of cold coffee for three days. Not because I forgot it—I see it every morning when I reach for the orange juice. I simply haven't decided whether to drink it, pour it out, or wash it. This small indecision has become oddly comforting, a tiny pocket of incompleteness in a life that desperately wants everything resolved.

We live in an age of completion. Finish the project, close the loop, achieve closure, reach your goals, check the boxes. Every productivity guru, self-help book, and motivational podcast insists that the uncompleted is the unresolved, and the unresolved is the problematic. There's a reason we call them "loose ends." They feel chaotic, like a thread hanging from a sweater that might unravel everything if we pull it.

But I wonder if we've gotten something fundamentally wrong about what matters in life.

Last week, I was talking to my friend Marcus about a novel he's been writing for six years. He has about eighty thousand words written, multiple character arcs developed, a clear ending in mind. And yet he hasn't touched it in months. When I asked why, expecting to hear about some creative block or practical obstacle, he said something unexpected: "I think I'm afraid to finish it because then I'd have to accept that it's not perfect, and I'd have to let it go into the world as it actually is, not as I imagined it could be."

This hit me harder than it probably should have. Because what he was describing wasn't really about writing—it was about the fundamental human experience of living in possibility. As long as the novel is unfinished, it exists in potential. It could be the best thing he's ever written. It could change everything. The moment he completes it, submits it, publishes it, he has to accept its actual limitations. He has to live with the reality rather than the promise.

I think about my own life constantly through this lens now. How much of my anxiety comes not from actual failures but from the gap between what I could potentially accomplish and what I've actually accomplished? The gap is where the shame lives. The gap is where we tell ourselves we're not trying hard enough, being good enough, doing enough. The gap is uncomfortable, yes, but it's also where hope lives. And maybe those are the same place.

Consider the way we treat relationships. We speak about "closure" as though it's a destination we need to reach with every person who passes through our lives. We agonize over unanswered questions, unresolved conflicts, words we didn't say. Some of this is legitimate—there are things that genuinely need to be addressed, conversations that need to happen. But I've noticed how often we torture ourselves over the fact that we can never fully explain ourselves to another person, never make sure they understand us completely, never know if we left a good final impression.

What if that incompleteness is actually the basis of all human connection?

I have a theory that we fall in love not with people as they are, but with people as they are *becoming*. We fall in love with possibility. The person your partner might become, the depths you haven't yet discovered in them, the ways they might surprise you ten years in. The moment you think you've fully understood someone, you've already stopped really seeing them. Real people are always unfinished. Real people are always essays in progress, not final submissions.

My parents have been married for forty-three years, and when I asked my mother recently if she feels like she knows my father completely, she laughed in a way that was both sad and joyful. "God, no," she said. "I'm constantly discovering things about him that contradict things I thought I knew. It drives me crazy sometimes. But I think that's the whole point. The day you think you've figured someone out is the day you stop being curious about them."

This applies to ourselves as well. We're so focused on finding our "authentic self," our final form, the real version of us that we'll be when we get everything together. But what if there is no final version? What if the point isn't to reach some stable endpoint where we've figured everything out, but rather to learn to be okay with the fact that we're always going to be confusing, contradictory, and incomplete?

I've been thinking about this a lot in the context of aging. We're encouraged to see aging as a process of decline, a slow completion of our lives in the worst possible direction. But I notice that older people—the ones who seem genuinely content—rarely talk about their lives as though they're winding down. They talk about them as though they're still being written. My grandmother, at eighty-seven, still debates with my grandfather about things, still changes her mind about decisions she made years ago, still surprises herself with reactions she didn't expect to have.

"I thought I'd be done learning by now," she said to me once. "Isn't that funny? I've lived most of my life, and I'm still regularly confused about what things mean."

There's something liberating about that admission. Something that makes me want to stop rushing toward completion and instead develop a tolerance for unfinished business.

I think about the projects I've abandoned. Stories I started but never finished. Skills I began learning and then set aside. I used to feel shame about these abandoned things, seeing them as evidence of my inconstancy, my lack of follow-through. But I've recently started thinking about them differently. What if they weren't failures? What if they were just experiences that changed me and then naturally concluded? What if the point of starting something isn't always to finish it?

This was the hardest lesson to learn because it flies directly in the face of how I was raised. I was raised to finish what you start, to see projects through, to not be a quitter. These aren't bad values, exactly, but they can become tyrannical. They can transform life into one long to-do list, where peace is only possible when every item is crossed off—which, of course, it never is, because there are always more items.

I read somewhere that the Japanese have a word—*ma*—that refers to the space between things, the pause, the emptiness. And that this emptiness isn't negative; it's actually essential to the meaning of the things around it. Without silence, there would be no music. Without space, there would be no room. Without the pause between heartbeats, the heart wouldn't work.

I wonder if the same applies to our lives. Without the unfinished, without the pause, without the gaps—maybe there would be no meaning. Maybe we need the ongoing projects, the perpetual questions, the relationships that never quite become fully knowable, the growth that never quite completes.

This doesn't mean we shouldn't try to accomplish things. It doesn't mean we shouldn't set goals and work toward them. It's not an argument for laziness or complacency. It's just an argument for being less violent about our relationship to completion. For understanding that some of the most important things in life are by definition unfinishable.

Take parenting, for instance. You never finish being a parent. Your children become adults and you're still figuring it out, still wondering if you did it right, still discovering new ways you've affected them. There's no graduation ceremony where you turn in a complete project. And this should be terrifying, probably, but instead I find it oddly beautiful. The incompleteness isn't a flaw in the system—it's the entire point.

Or consider something like learning a language, or learning to play music. The common wisdom is that you should aim to achieve fluency or mastery, as though these are destinations you can reach and then be done. But musicians and linguists who genuinely love what they do don't talk about it that way. They talk about the endless discovery, the way that learning to play a new piece always teaches you something about the instrument you didn't know before, the way a language is always revealing new depths and nuances.

The best students I've ever encountered are people who became genuinely comfortable with not knowing. Not because they didn't care about learning, but because they understood that absolute mastery would mean the end of the interesting part. The growth would stop. The discovery would end. And that would be terrible.

I have a friend who practices yoga, and she told me something her teacher said that stuck with me: "The posture is never complete. There's always a deeper level, a better alignment, a subtler awareness you can bring to it. And that's not discouraging—it's the whole point. It means you'll never be bored. It means there's always more to discover about your own body, your own being."

This seems like the opposite of how we usually think about skill acquisition. We want to reach competence and then move on to the next thing. But there's something to be said for the practice of deepening, for the willingness to spend years in the same space, discovering new dimensions of it.

I've been trying to apply this to my own anxiety about productivity. I'm a person who has internalized the cultural narrative about constant improvement and self-optimization to an almost pathological degree. I have spreadsheets tracking my habits. I have systems for organizing my time. I measure my worth somewhat unconsciously against how much I accomplish. This has gotten me some things—some real achievements, some genuine successes. But it's also kept me in a state of low-level anxiety that I'm not doing enough, being enough, becoming enough.

What if, instead of trying to optimize my way to peace, I just... stopped? Not in the sense of giving up, but in the sense of being willing to have an afternoon where I don't accomplish anything and simply exist. An evening where I don't learn anything. A day where I'm not becoming a better version of myself.

This feels radical because we've been taught that time is a scarce resource we need to maximize. Every moment not spent improving ourselves is, by this logic, wasted. But what if the wasted moments are the most important ones? What if doing nothing is sometimes the most powerful thing you can do?

I'm thinking about this partly because I've been spending more time outside lately, just sitting and watching things. Not meditating in the purposeful, self-improving sense, but just being present without agenda. And I've noticed that these are often the times when something shifts in me. When I suddenly understand something I've been struggling with. When a problem that seemed urgent suddenly loses its urgency. When I feel more like myself than I do when I'm actively trying to be better.

Maybe the trick is that you have to let go of trying to improve in order to actually change. Maybe all the pushing and striving is actually counterproductive. Maybe we're supposed to unfold gradually, without constant intervention, like a flower.

I don't have answers to any of this. I'm sitting with questions. And increasingly, I'm okay with that. The questions feel more interesting to me now than the answers would be. An answered question is a dead question. A living question is one you can keep asking in different ways, getting slightly different answers each time, discovering that the question itself changes as you change.

So my coffee is still sitting there, half-full, and I think I'm going to leave it. Not forever—eventually I'll throw it out or drink it or wash the mug. But for now, it sits there as a small monument to incompleteness, a reminder that it's okay to not know what happens next. That some decisions don't need to be made immediately. That some things can exist in a state of pleasant suspension.

And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's everything.
